This Lake Superior shoreline becomes the Apostle Islands Ice Caves in the winter, so you can stroll right in where you have to swim (if you have a wetsuit to handle the cold water) in the summer.

In Wisconsin where I live now, the ice caves that Apostle Islands National Lakeshore is known for used to be accessible almost every winter. The ice on Lake Superior hasn't been thick enough for hiking to them to be safe since 2015.

The ice caves are a natural phenomenon at the Apostle Islands National Lakeshore, a federally protected, 12-mile shoreline of Lake Superior that includes 21 islands, at the northern tip of Wisconsin's Bayfield Peninsula.
For the first time in 11 years, the Apostle Islands ice caves will open but rangers warn that conditions can change rapidly on Lake Superior. Details

Good examples of the sea caves of the Great Lakes are located on the shorelines of the Apostle Islands. Arches and delicate chambers are visible. During the winters, visitors can see frozen waterfalls and chambers filled with delicate icicles. #wisconsin

The Apostle Island ice caves on Lake Superior, which reopened on Monday for the first time since 2015, are closing on Tuesday due to a winter storm. They could remain closed for several days as conditions are evaluated.
Before this week, the last time conditions allowed access to the caves along Lake Superior in Apostle Islands National Lakeshore was in 2015.

Getting to the Apostle Islands ice caves in Wisconsin requires a multi-mile trek over the frozen surface of Lake Superior. This week, a handful of lucky visitors got the chance to see them. Read more at the link in comments.
